human: Photosynthesis is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy — typically from sunlight — into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism. The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting. Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds, typically carbohydrates like sugars, starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose. When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration. Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of the Earth's atmosphere, and it supplies most of the biological energy necessary for complex life on Earth.

Quantum mechanics, also known as quantum physics, is the fundamental physical theory that describes the behavior of matter and of light; its unusual characteristics typically occur at and below the scale of atoms. Its concepts and methods have been applied across many disciplines, including quantum chemistry, quantum biology, quantum field theory, quantum technology, and quantum information science.

A black hole is an astronomical body so compact that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping. Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, which describes gravitation as the curvature of spacetime, predicts that any sufficiently compact mass will form a black hole. The boundary of no escape is called the event horizon. In general relativity, crossing a black hole's event horizon traps an object inside but produces no locally detectable change. General relativity also predicts that every black hole should have a central singularity, where the curvature of spacetime is infinite.

General relativity, also known as the general theory of relativity, and as Einstein's theory of gravity, is the geometric theory of gravitation published by Albert Einstein in May 1916 and is the accepted description of the gravitation of macroscopic objects in modern physics. General relativity generalizes special relativity and refines Isaac Newton's law of universal gravitation, providing a unified description of gravity as a geometric property of space and time, or four-dimensional spacetime. In particular, the curvature of spacetime is directly related to the energy, momentum, and stress of whatever is present, including matter and radiation. The relation is specified by the Einstein field equations, a system of second-order partial differential equations. John Archibald Wheeler summarized it: "Space-time tells matter how to move; matter tells space-time how to curve."

Thermodynamics is a branch of physics that deals with heat, work, and temperature, and their relation to energy, entropy, and the physical properties of matter and radiation. The behavior of these quantities is governed by the four laws of thermodynamics, which convey a quantitative description using measurable macroscopic physical quantities but may be explained in terms of microscopic constituents by statistical mechanics. Thermodynamics applies to various topics in science and engineering, especially physical chemistry, biochemistry, chemical engineering, and mechanical engineering, as well as other complex fields such as meteorology.

In physics, electromagnetism is an interaction that occurs between particles with electric charge via electromagnetic fields. The electromagnetic force is one of the four fundamental forces of nature. It is the dominant force in the interactions of atoms and molecules. Electromagnetism describes and relates the three distinct but closely intertwined phenomena of electricity, magnetism, and optics. In, electromagnetism these phenomena are described by the 3 sub-disciplines: electrostatics, magnetostatics, and electrodynamics.

The periodic table, also known as the periodic table of the elements, is an ordered arrangement of the chemical elements into rows ("periods") and columns ("groups"). An icon of chemistry, the periodic table is widely used in physics and other sciences. It is a depiction of the periodic law, which states that when the elements are arranged in order of their atomic numbers an approximate recurrence of their properties is evident. The table is divided into four roughly rectangular areas called blocks. Elements in the same group tend to show similar chemical characteristics.

The Standard Model of particle physics is the theory describing three of the four known fundamental forces in the universe and classifying all known elementary particles. It was developed in stages throughout the latter half of the 20th century, through the work of many scientists worldwide, with the current formulation being finalized in the mid-1970s upon experimental confirmation of the existence of quarks. Since then, proof of the top quark (1995), the tau neutrino (2000), and the Higgs boson (2012) have added further credence to the Standard Model. In addition, the Standard Model has predicted with great accuracy the various properties of weak neutral currents and the W and Z bosons.

This process occurs in chloroplasts, using chlorophyll pigments to capture photons. **Quantum mechanics** is a fundamental theory in physics that describes the physical properties of nature at the smallest scales—typically at the level of atoms and subatomic particles. It departs from classical mechanics by introducing concepts such as wave–particle duality, where particles exhibit both particle-like and wave-like behaviors, and the uncertainty principle, which posits limits on how precisely certain pairs of physical properties (e.g., position and momentum) can be known simultaneously. The theory is built on a mathematical framework using state vectors in Hilbert space, with observable quantities represented by operators. Its predictions, often probabilistic, are confirmed by phenomena like quantization of energy levels and quantum entanglement. Quantum mechanics underpins much of modern technology, including semiconductors, lasers, and quantum computing, and remains one of the most successful and rigorously tested theories in science.

A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so intense that nothing—not even light—can escape. Formed when a massive star collapses under its own gravity at the end of its life cycle, it creates a singularity, a point of infinite density, surrounded by an event horizon—the boundary beyond which no matter or radiation can exit. Predicted by Einstein's theory of general relativity in 1916, the term "black hole" was coined by physicist John Archibald Wheeler in 1967. While invisible, black holes are detected by their gravitational effects on nearby stars and gas, and by the X-rays emitted from material spiraling into them. They vary in size from stellar-mass black holes (a few solar masses) to supermassive ones, found at the centers of most galaxies, containing millions to billions of solar masses. Their study remains a cornerstone of modern astrophysics.

**General relativity** is a fundamental theory in physics describing gravity, formulated by Albert Einstein in 1915. It revolutionized the understanding of gravitation by depicting it not as a force, as in Isaac Newton's theory, but as a curvature of spacetime caused by the presence of mass and energy. This curvature dictates the motion of objects, which follow geodesic paths through the four-dimensional spacetime continuum. Key predictions of the theory include the bending of light by gravity, gravitational time dilation, the existence of black holes, and the expansion of the universe. General relativity has been rigorously tested through experiments and observations, such as the precise precession of Mercury’s orbit and the detection of gravitational waves, and remains a cornerstone of modern astrophysics and cosmology.

**Thermodynamics** is a branch of physics concerned with heat, work, temperature, and their interrelation with energy and physical properties of matter. It originated from the study of steam engines in the 19th century and has since developed into a fundamental framework governing all energy conversions. The discipline is built upon a set of universal laws: the zeroth law establishes thermal equilibrium; the first law formalizes the conservation of energy; the second law defines the irreversibility of natural processes and the increase of entropy; and the third law sets an absolute zero limit for temperature. Thermodynamics is essential to fields such as chemistry, engineering, biology, and cosmology, providing the theoretical basis for engines, refrigerators, chemical reactions, and the behavior of stars.

**Electromagnetism** is a fundamental branch of physics that studies the interactions between electrically charged particles and magnetic fields. It unifies electricity and magnetism as manifestations of a single underlying phenomenon, described mathematically by James Clerk Maxwell's equations in the 19th century. These equations predict that electric and magnetic fields propagate as waves—electromagnetic radiation—at the speed of light, linking electromagnetism to optics. The theory governs phenomena from atomic bonding to planetary magnetism, and its practical applications include electric motors, telecommunications, and medical imaging. Electromagnetism is one of the four fundamental forces of nature, essential for understanding matter, energy, and the structure of the universe.

The periodic table is a tabular arrangement of the chemical elements, organized by increasing atomic number and grouped into rows (periods) and columns (groups) based on recurring chemical and physical properties. First systematically presented by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, it allows for the prediction of element behavior through periodic trends. The modern table, refined by Henry Moseley, classifies elements into blocks (s, p, d, f) and highlights similarities within groups. It is a foundational tool in chemistry and physics, illustrating atomic structure, bonding, and reactivity.

The Standard Model is the prevailing theoretical framework describing the fundamental particles and the three of the four known forces (electromagnetism, the weak force, and the strong force) that govern their interactions, excluding gravity. Developed in the mid-20th century, it is a quantum field theory that classifies elementary particles into fermions (matter particles, like quarks and leptons) and bosons (force carriers, including photons, gluons, and the W and Z bosons). Its predictions, including the existence of the Higgs boson—confirmed experimentally in 2012—have been validated with high precision. Despite its successes, the model is incomplete, as it does not incorporate gravity, explain dark matter, or account for neutrino masses fully, prompting searches for physics beyond it.

Electromagnetism is a core area of physics that looks at how electrically charged particles interact with magnetic fields. Electromagnetism ranks as one of nature’s four fundamental forces, and it’s key to making sense of matter, energy, and how the universe is put together.

The periodic table is a structured layout of the chemical elements, sorted by rising atomic number and arranged into horizontal rows called periods and vertical columns known as groups, all based on repeating chemical and physical traits. It was first put together in an organized way by Dmitri Mendeleev back in 1869, making it possible to predict how elements behave by looking at periodic trends. This table is a cornerstone of both chemistry and physics, helping to explain atomic structure, how atoms bond, and their reactivity.

It describes the elementary particles and how they interact via three of the four known fundamental forces—electromagnetism, the weak nuclear force, and the strong nuclear force—but it leaves out gravity. Developed during the mid-20th century, it’s built on quantum field theory and sorts particles into two main categories: fermions, which are the building blocks of matter (like quarks and leptons), and bosons, which are the carriers of force (such as photons, gluons, and the W and Z bosons). Its predictions have held up under rigorous testing, and the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012, which the model had predicted, was a major experimental confirmation.
